body:
Understanding a map

A map is a representation of the whole Earth or a part of its surface on a flat surface, drawn according to a scale and using appropriate symbols. It presents geographical features as viewed from above.

A map cannot reproduce every feature of the Earth's surface. The features included depend on the purpose of the map, the size of the area represented and the scale selected. For example, a village map may show individual houses, wells, agricultural fields and roads, whereas a world map usually shows only major geographical features.

The art and science of making and studying maps is called cartography. The process of selecting and simplifying geographical information according to the scale and purpose of a map is called map generalisation.

Map, globe, sketch and plan

RepresentationMain characteristic
GlobeA three-dimensional model of the Earth
MapA scaled representation on a flat surface
SketchA rough drawing without an accurate scale
PlanA detailed drawing of a small area at a large scale

A globe represents the overall shape of the Earth more faithfully than a flat world map. However, maps are easier to carry, reproduce and use for examining small areas in detail. A collection of maps published together is called an atlas.

Essential components of a map

The basic components used in elementary map reading are distance, direction and symbols. Other information, such as the title, projection and legend, helps the reader interpret the map correctly.

  • Title: Identifies the geographical area or subject represented.
  • Scale: Establishes the relationship between map distance and ground distance.
  • Direction: Helps determine the relative positions of places.
  • Symbols: Represent geographical features in a simplified form.
  • Legend or key: Explains the meaning of symbols, colours and patterns.
  • Projection: Provides a systematic method of representing the curved Earth on a flat surface.

Classification according to purpose

Physical or relief maps

Physical maps primarily represent natural geographical features such as mountains, plateaus, plains, rivers, lakes and oceans. Relief maps specifically emphasise differences in elevation and the shape of the land surface.

Political maps

Political maps primarily represent administrative and territorial divisions, including countries, states, districts, boundaries, capitals and important cities.

Thematic maps

A thematic map represents the geographical distribution of a particular subject, such as rainfall, population density, soil types, forests, industries or agricultural crops.

A thematic map may deal with either a physical subject, such as rainfall, or a human subject, such as literacy. Therefore, thematic maps are not restricted to human geography.

Topographical maps

Topographical maps provide detailed information about both natural and human-made features of an area. They show relief, drainage, vegetation, settlements, roads, railways and other features through contours and conventional symbols.

Cadastral maps

Cadastral maps represent individual land parcels and property boundaries at a very large scale. They are useful for land ownership records, land administration and revenue purposes.

General-purpose and special-purpose maps

A general-purpose map provides several types of geographical information together. A topographical map is an example. A special-purpose or thematic map concentrates on a selected subject, such as the distribution of rainfall.

Prelims focus

  • Cartography is the art and science of map-making.
  • An atlas is a collection of maps.
  • A sketch does not maintain an accurate scale.
  • Cadastral maps show land parcels and property boundaries.
  • Topographical maps represent natural and human-made features.
  • Trap: A rainfall map is a thematic map even though rainfall is a natural phenomenon.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018-19, Chapter 4, Maps, pp. 23-29; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Introduction to Maps, pp. 1-12; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 15, Maps: Meaning and Types, pp. 111-115, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Maps, Globes and Types of Maps

body:
Meaning of scale

Geographical areas are generally much larger than the maps used to represent them. A map must therefore reduce actual ground distances in a systematic manner.

Map scale is the ratio of a distance measured on a map to the corresponding horizontal distance on the ground, expressed in the same units.

For example, if 1 cm on a map represents 1 km on the ground, the map reduces the corresponding ground distance by a factor of 100,000 because 1 km equals 100,000 cm.

Methods of expressing scale

Statement or verbal scale

A statement scale expresses the relationship between map distance and ground distance in words or measurement units.

Example: 1 cm represents 500 m. This means that every centimetre measured on the map corresponds to 500 m on the ground.

Representative fraction

A representative fraction, abbreviated as RF, expresses scale as a numerical ratio or fraction. Both distances must be expressed in the same unit.

For example, a scale of 1:50,000 means that 1 unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground.

  • The numerator represents map distance.
  • The denominator represents the corresponding ground distance.
  • The ratio has no measurement unit of its own.

Thus, 1:50,000 means 1 cm represents 50,000 cm, or 1 mm represents 50,000 mm. The representative fraction can be used with any consistent system of length measurement.

Graphical or linear scale

A graphical scale, also called a bar scale, uses a graduated line or bar to represent actual ground distances. The reader compares a measured map distance with the divisions marked on the scale bar.

A bar scale may contain major divisions marked in kilometres and smaller subdivisions for reading distances in metres.

Comparison of scale methods

MethodExampleMain characteristic
Statement1 cm represents 500 mEasy to understand
RF1:50,000Independent of measurement units
GraphicalGraduated kilometre barRemains valid after proportional resizing

If a map is enlarged or reduced uniformly together with its graphical scale, the scale bar changes in the same proportion as the map. It therefore continues to represent the correct relationship between distances.

The original statement scale and representative fraction, however, become incorrect after resizing unless their values are recalculated.

A graphical scale remains valid when both the map and the scale bar are enlarged or reduced uniformly. This advantage does not apply if the map is stretched unequally or the scale bar is resized separately.

Large-scale and small-scale maps

The size of a map scale is determined by the numerical value of its representative fraction, not by the physical dimensions of the sheet on which the map is printed.

A map with a scale of 1:50,000 has a larger scale than a map with a scale of 1:500,000 because the fraction 1/50,000 is greater than 1/500,000.

CharacteristicLarge-scale mapSmall-scale map
RF denominatorSmallerLarger
Ground area on an equal-sized sheetSmallerLarger
Geographical detailUsually greaterUsually less
ExamplesVillage maps, cadastral mapsWorld maps, atlas maps

At 1:50,000, a map width of 4 cm represents 2 km on the ground. At 1:500,000, the same map width represents 20 km. The first map can show a smaller area in greater detail, whereas the second must simplify its geographical information.

Prelims focus

  • Scale is the ratio of map distance to corresponding ground distance.
  • Statement scale, representative fraction and graphical scale are the 3 main methods of expressing scale.
  • RF is a dimensionless ratio.
  • A smaller RF denominator indicates a larger scale.
  • Graphical scales remain valid when maps and scale bars are resized proportionally.
  • Trap: A physically larger printed map does not necessarily have a larger scale.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Introduction to Maps, pp. 7-8, and Chapter 2, Map Scale, pp. 17-21; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 15, pp. 112-114, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Map Scale and Its Forms

body:
Units used in map calculations

Map-scale calculations require consistent units. The most useful metric conversions are:

  • 1 km = 1,000 m.
  • 1 m = 100 cm.
  • 1 km = 100,000 cm.
  • 1 cm = 10 mm.

Calculating ground distance

When a map has a representative fraction of 1:N, each unit measured on the map represents N of the same units on the ground.

$$\text{Ground distance}=\text{Map distance}\times N$$

Distance calculation

Two places are separated by 6 cm on a map drawn at 1:50,000.

Ground distance = 6 × 50,000 cm = 300,000 cm.

Since 100,000 cm equals 1 km, the actual horizontal distance is 3 km.

Calculating map distance

When ground distance and scale are known, divide the ground distance by the denominator of the representative fraction. Convert the units before performing the calculation.

$$\text{Map distance}=\frac{\text{Ground distance}}{N}$$

For example, 4 km equals 400,000 cm. On a map of scale 1:100,000, this distance is represented by 4 cm.

Converting between statement scale and RF

To convert a statement scale into a representative fraction, express the map distance and ground distance in identical units and reduce the ratio so that its numerator becomes 1.

If 2 cm represents 5 km:

  • 5 km = 500,000 cm.
  • RF = 2:500,000.
  • After dividing both terms by 2, RF = 1:250,000.

To convert RF into a statement scale, express the denominator in a convenient ground-distance unit. A scale of 1:25,000 means that 1 cm represents 25,000 cm, or 250 m.

Common representative fractions

Map scaleGround distance represented by 1 cm
1:1,00010 m
1:10,000100 m
1:25,000250 m
1:50,000500 m
1:100,0001 km
1:250,0002.5 km
1:1,000,00010 km

Straight-line distance and route distance

The straight-line distance between 2 places is not necessarily the distance travelled along a road, railway or river.

A straight-line map distance can be measured using a ruler. To measure a curved feature, such as a winding river or road, a flexible thread may be placed along the feature and then straightened against a ruler or scale bar.

Consider an imaginary route from A to C through B on a map of scale 1:50,000. The distance from A to B is 3 cm, from B to C is 4 cm and the direct distance from A to C is 5 cm.

  • Direct distance from A to C = 5 × 0.5 km = 2.5 km.
  • Route distance through B = (3 + 4) × 0.5 km = 3.5 km.

The route is longer because it follows the connecting road rather than the shortest straight line between the endpoints.

Scale and area

A map scale relates linear distances. When calculating an area, the conversion applies to both length and width.

At a scale of 1:100,000, 1 cm represents 1 km. A rectangular area measuring 2 cm by 3 cm on the map therefore represents a ground area of 2 km by 3 km, equal to 6 km2.

Similarly, a square measuring 1 cm by 1 cm on a map of scale 1:50,000 represents 500 m by 500 m, or 0.25 km2.

Ordinary map-scale measurements represent horizontal distances. The actual distance travelled along steep or uneven ground may be greater. On maps covering very large regions, projection distortion may also affect distance measurements.

Prelims focus

  • 1 km equals 100,000 cm.
  • At 1:50,000, 1 cm represents 500 m.
  • Ground distance is obtained by multiplying map distance by the RF denominator.
  • A thread can be used to measure a winding route.
  • Area calculations require conversion of both linear dimensions.
  • Trap: Straight-line distance and travelling distance are not necessarily equal.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018-19, Chapter 4, Maps, pp. 24-25; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Measurement of Distance and Area, pp. 13-14, and Chapter 2, Map Scale, pp. 17-21.]

title: Measuring Distance and Using Map Scales

body:
Cardinal and intermediate directions

Direction describes the position of one place relative to another. The 4 principal directions, known as cardinal directions, are north, east, south and west.

The intermediate directions lie between adjacent cardinal directions:

  • Northeast lies between north and east.
  • Southeast lies between south and east.
  • Southwest lies between south and west.
  • Northwest lies between north and west.

Maps commonly indicate north using an arrow marked N. On a north-up map, north is towards the top, south towards the bottom, east towards the right and west towards the left. However, not every map is oriented with north at the top.

Direction as a relative position

When describing direction, identify the reference point first. The direction of A from B is measured from B towards A.

If a village lies northeast of a town, the town lies southwest of the village. Reversing the reference point reverses the direction.

DirectionOpposite direction
NorthSouth
EastWest
NortheastSouthwest
SoutheastNorthwest

Elementary bearings

A bearing describes direction as an angle, usually measured clockwise from north. It provides a more precise description than a cardinal or intermediate direction alone.

North corresponds to 0° or 360°, east to 90°, south to 180° and west to 270°. Northeast corresponds to 45°, southeast to 135°, southwest to 225° and northwest to 315°.

These angular relationships help identify directions even when a question represents them using numerical bearings.

Compass and north direction

A magnetic compass is an instrument that indicates direction using a magnetised needle. Its needle aligns approximately with the local magnetic field of the Earth.

True north is the direction towards the geographical North Pole. Magnetic north is the northward direction indicated by a magnetic compass. The 2 directions do not necessarily coincide.

Locating places with latitude and longitude

Latitude and longitude provide a geographical coordinate system for locating places on the Earth. The network formed by parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude is called a graticule.

  • Latitude: Expresses angular position north or south of the Equator. The Equator is 0° latitude, while the poles are 90° north and 90° south.
  • Longitude: Expresses angular position east or west of the Prime Meridian, which is 0° longitude.

Parallels of latitude generally extend east-west around the globe, although latitude values describe north-south position. Meridians of longitude extend from pole to pole, although longitude values describe east-west position.

Within a small region, coordinates can be compared to determine the approximate relative directions of places. Consider 3 imaginary locations:

  • A: 20°N, 70°E.
  • B: 22°N, 70°E.
  • C: 22°N, 72°E.

B lies north of A because it has a higher northern latitude and the same longitude. C lies east of B because it has a higher eastern longitude and the same latitude. C lies approximately northeast of A.

The ground distance represented by 1° of longitude decreases towards the poles because the meridians converge. Consequently, equal differences in longitude do not represent equal ground distances at different latitudes.

Prelims focus

  • North, east, south and west are the cardinal directions.
  • Bearings are normally measured clockwise from north.
  • East corresponds to a bearing of 90°.
  • Latitude describes north-south position; longitude describes east-west position.
  • Meridians converge towards the poles.
  • Trap: The top of a map is not automatically north. Check the orientation.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018-19, Chapter 4, Maps, pp. 24-25; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 6, Chapter 1, Locating Places on the Earth, pp. 10-15; NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 1, Measurement of Direction, p. 14; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 16, pp. 117-120, consulted 26 November 2026.]
